svg.title: Isolation domains and governed boundary crossing
svg.desc: A mobile-first Agent Memory diagram showing multiple logical memory isolation domains inside one physical store. The same agent may work in Project A Task 1, Project B Task 2, and a shared security space without receiving automatic authority to move memory among them. A highly relevant cross-domain candidate must resolve the target domain, current membership, scope, purpose, destination, consent or delegation, sensitivity, and revocation state before PAMA evaluates the crossing. Blocked crossings remain blocked regardless of relevance. Permitted crossings use an allowed representation and produce a reconstructable receipt. Derived state keeps inherited source constraints, and later correction, revocation, scope reduction, or purge may create propagation obligations.
svg.text: Isolation domains and governed crossing
One physical store can hold many logical authority boundaries.
HARD INVARIANTS
physical store != isolation domain
same agent != same memory scope
relevance != permission to cross
A perfect semantic match cannot authorize another domain.
01 SHARED PHYSICAL SUBSTRATE
One store, three governed domains
The storage service is shared. Authority is not.
Project A / Task 1
project-local memory boundary
Project B / Task 2
separate project and task authority
Shared security space
broader membership, still a governed isolation domain
The same agent may participate in all three without free memory flow.
02 CANDIDATE OR CROSSING REQUEST
Useful does not mean reachable
Agent is operating in Project A / Task 1.
Retriever discovers a Project B / Task 2 memory.
semantic relevance = 1.0 · same agent = true
source domain != target domain => crossing requires governance
03 RESOLVE TARGET DOMAIN + CURRENT AUTHORITY
Establish what boundary authorizes use now
principal / actor · target isolation domain · project / task · purpose
membership · consent / delegation · sensitivity · destination
re-sharing policy · expiry / revocation · policy version
Membership creates eligibility, not automatic admission.
Unknown or ambiguous scope does not become broad permission.
Unresolved authority must block, narrow, verify, or require review.
current authority beats prior access, identity, and relevance
04 PAMA EVALUATES THE CROSSING CONSEQUENCE
Source authorization does not authorize destination use
source domain · destination domain · fan-out / audience expansion
purpose change · sensitivity · persistence · reversibility
representation · shared/canonical status · downstream authority
PAMA resolves the permitted consequence envelope.
Prior source approval, high confidence, saturation, or retrieval score
cannot silently relax the destination authority requirement.
read authorized != export authorized != scope-promotion authority
05 GOVERNED OUTCOME
Only a permitted treatment may cross
Blocked path
block · require review · require verification · narrow destination
Permitted path
raw · redacted · summary-only · other policy-permitted representation
The selected treatment must stay inside the permitted action set.
A blocked crossing is not reopened by a stronger semantic score.
06 CROSSING RECEIPT
Make the decision reconstructable
operation · source / destination domains · actor / principal · purpose
representation · sensitivity · consent / delegation · PAMA outcome
policy version · provenance · expiry / revocation · receipt ID
A receipt proves the bound decision, not permanent future validity.
later authority changes can create new lifecycle obligations
07 DERIVED STATE + LIFECYCLE PROPAGATION
Transformation does not erase inherited authority or provenance.
Correction, revocation, scope reduction, or purge may propagate across
authorized crossings and downstream derived state where policy requires.
